new_statements.quote: Os seguintes exemplos Miguelenho ilustram as representações arbóreas permitidas nas línguas Chapakura: [mă'wĩn] 'urucum', [mă'wi:] 'roubar', ['pĩʔ] 'dançar', ['pi:] 'espinho' ... uma sílaba pesada caracteriza sempre o final de um lexema [p.23] ... Nas línguas Chapakura, a acentuação dos lexemas é dedutível do peso silábico - o único fator prosódico fonológico nessa família lingüística. Portanto, o acento não é fonológico por ser previsível. ... (a) uma sílaba leve é átona e possui um tom baixo ... (b) uma sílaba pesada é tônica e possui um tom alto. Em outras palavras, carrega um acento de intensidade ('stress') forte e um acento de altura ('pitch') alto. /#(σ)σ#/ → [(σ̀)ˈσ́] [p.24] ... (c) em Miguelenho-Wanham ... É a intensidade maior que é preservada na modalidade 'frágil', globalmente ..., enquanto que se manteve na sua versão 'resistente', quando o 'onset' do lexema é uma oclusão glotal. Quanto à altura maior, manteve-se na sua modalidade 'resistente', globalmente [p.168 = ILLA p.156]
new_statements.translation: The following Miguelenho examples illustrate the tree representations permitted in the Chapakura languages: [mă'wĩn] 'annatto', [mă'wi:] 'to steal', ['pĩʔ] 'to dance', ['pi:] 'thorn' ... a heavy syllable always characterizes the end of a lexeme ... In the Chapakura languages, lexeme accentuation is deducible from syllable weight - the only phonological prosodic factor in this family. Hence accent is not phonological, being predictable. ... (a) a light syllable is unstressed and low-toned ... (b) a heavy syllable is stressed and high-toned, i.e. it carries strong intensity accent ('stress') and high pitch accent. /#(σ)σ#/ -> [(σ̀)ˈσ́] ... (c) in Miguelenho-Wanham ... it is the greater intensity [on the heavy syllable] that is preserved in the 'fragile' mode globally, while it remained 'resistant' when the lexeme onset is a glottal stop; the higher pitch remained 'resistant' globally.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Lexemes are monosyllabic (one heavy syllable CVC/CV:/CVV) or disyllabic (light CV + heavy); stress (intensity and high pitch) falls on the heavy syllable, i.e. the final syllable of every lexeme, and is fully predictable from syllable weight, hence non-contrastive. For Miguelenho-Wanyam specifically the authors' acoustic measurements (last speaker) show the heavy final syllable carrying the pitch prominence robustly and the intensity prominence more weakly ('frágil', i.e. as the end of a plateau) except after a glottal-stop onset.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; the light first syllable of a disyllable is 'átona' with low tone (notation [(σ̀)ˈσ́] marks it low, not secondarily stressed).
new_statements.exceptions: In casual/hypoarticulated registers vowel shortening and fusion of monosyllabic lexemes can merge up to three lexemes into one phonological word (rule 2, p.23-24); the demarcation rule holds unconditionally only in maxi-articulated speech. Instrumentally, Miguelenho intensity prominence is 'frágil' (plateau-final) when the lexeme onset is not a glottal stop.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the lexeme (= morphological word; the languages are analysed as fully isolating, lexemes mono- or disyllabic); compounds/polylexical words are sequences of such lexemes each ending in a stressed heavy syllable. Data are citation forms from the last Miguelenho-Wanyam speaker recorded by Angenot-de Lima (CEPLA acoustic archive 1997b). The rule is stated for the family ('línguas Chapakura') and instantiated with Miguelenho examples and Miguelenho-specific acoustic results.
new_statements.identity_note: The statement rests on Angenot-de Lima's first-hand data from the last speaker of 'Miguelenho-Wanyam' (= Wanham/Wañam of the rio São Miguel, Guajará-Mirim region, recorded mid-1990s). Glottolog files Ribeiro 1998 'Léxico Português/Miguelenho' under wany1246 and Birchall et al. 2016 treat Miguelenho, Cabixi (Hanke 1975) and Abitana (Snethlage/Loukotka 1963) as dialects/subgroups of Wanyam, so the identity with wany1246 is direct. The rule itself is formulated family-wide ('línguas Chapakura') and instantiated with Miguelenho examples (p.23 / ILLA p.150) plus a Miguelenho-specific instrumental result (p.168 / ILLA p.156); Birchall et al. 2016 note that no detailed phonological description of Wanyam was completed before the last speaker died.
